doc.title: Curtis Fuller — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Army band at Fort Knox with Cannonball Adderley and Junior Mance
summary: Fuller dates his service to 1953-55 and describes the last all-black Army band at Fort Knox, with Cannonball as director without rank, Junior Mance as clerk, and Mel Wanzo.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Now, we got to…Well, that was what? 1950-what?
Well, when I got out it was ’55.
Okay, since we are there, who else was in that band? Junior Mance was in that band.
Junior Mance was the company clerk because he was the piano player. He had to play the glockenspiel, or whatever that thing is.
And what was that band called?
It was the 132nd Army band I figure. It was the 132nd or thirty something. It was the 3rd armored division.
They were in the process of de-segregating?

It was the last black army band, yeah. Slide Hampton’s brother, he was processed through there. They were, you know, I think the full script was 28. Everybody didn’t play a horn; they had many administrative people. Cannonball couldn’t be head of it because he wasn’t the warrant officer. They gave him a staff sergeant thing because they sent him up here to the Naval School of Music. He passed that course. He got to be the band director, but he wasn’t in charge. He couldn’t be because he was a staff sergeant. You had to be a warrant officer to be in charge and he was not that. Junior Mance got caught by a corporal because he was doing administrative things and that was (inaudible) and I was a new comer. Mel Wanzo and I-- Mel Wanzo was there for me. I don’t know if you know who Mel Wanzo is.
